claims.text: A point on the equator moves at about 1,670 km/h because of Earth's spin (Astronomy: 1,668 km/h; IFLScience: 1,670 km/h).
claims.quote: A point along the equator moves at approximately 1,037 mph (1,668 km/h); At the equator, it's like being in a car that was moving at 1,670 kilometers (1,038 miles) per hour; Equatorial radius (km) 6378.137; Sidereal rotation period (hrs) 23.9345
claims.note: Check from NASA's fact sheet: circumference 2 x pi x 6378.137 km = 40,075 km; one rotation takes 23.9345 h (sidereal), so 40,075 / 23.9345 = 1,674 km/h (Astronomy's 1,668 uses the 24 h solar day: 40,075/24 = 1,670). Speed falls with latitude (x cos latitude); zero at the poles.

claims.text: If Earth stopped in an instant, the water, air and anything not anchored would keep moving at the speed of their latitude.
claims.quote: If Earth stopped spinning in an instant, all the water, air, and structures on Earth would still be moving at speeds corresponding to their latitudes; If the planet stopped suddenly, everything on the surface would be destroyed, as the atmosphere, oceans and anything not nailed down kept spinning

claims.text: After a sudden stop you would keep moving east (Earth spins eastward) and hit the nearest eastward wall.
claims.quote: If you are in a building you'll be thrown into the closest eastward wall

claims.text: The winds after a sudden stop would be about four times faster than the fastest wind ever recorded (408 km/h).
claims.quote: The winds alone would be four times faster and stronger than the fastest wind ever recorded ( 408 km/h 253 mph ); you'd experience wind speeds in excess of 1,000 mph, a velocity nearly five times greater in speed
claims.note: 1,670 / 408 = 4.1. Astronomy rounds the other way ('nearly five times'); the script says 'about four times'.

claims.text: After a sudden stop the oceans would keep moving and flood the coasts.
claims.quote: If Earth were to stop turning suddenly, that water would continue to move at a rapid velocity, inundating coastal and possibly even inner regions with a deluge of displaced ocean water

claims.text: Even if Earth slowed to a stop over several years, it would still be a disaster.
claims.quote: If it slowed down over several years, it would still be a disaster

claims.text: Because it spins, Earth bulges at the equator: the poles are about 21 km closer to the centre than the equator.
claims.quote: Due to its rotation, the Earth bulges in the middle, so the poles are about 21 kilometers (13 miles) closer to the center of the Earth than the equator; Equatorial radius (km) 6378.137; Polar radius (km) 6356.752; This oblateness results from the centrifugal force of the planet's rotation

claims.label: simplified model
claims.text: Without the spin, the oceans would move towards the poles, leaving two polar oceans and a belt of land around the middle; everything north of Spain would be underwater (a model, not a forecast).
claims.quote: Without centrifugal force, the oceans would move towards the poles, dropping ocean depth by 8km around the equator; Earth's water would be divided into two huge polar oceans separated by a belt of land in the middle. Everything north of Spain would be underwater, as well as all of Antarctica; Without the rotation, the oceans will migrate towards the poles
claims.note: IFLScience attributes the map to Witold Fraczek (Esri). Labelled 'simplified model' on the page.

claims.text: If Earth stopped spinning on its axis, one day would last a year: six months of daylight, then six months of night.
claims.quote: Once Earth doesn't spin on its own axis, a day lasts as long as a year. Everywhere receives six months of daylight; Sidereal orbit period (days) 365.256
claims.note: With no rotation relative to the stars, the Sun's position in the sky changes only because Earth orbits it, so one sunrise-to-sunrise cycle takes one orbit: 365.256 days (NASA). Half of that is daylight.

claims.label: BBC Science Focus estimate
claims.text: Six months of daylight would gradually heat the planet to well over 100°C (Science Focus estimate).
claims.quote: Everywhere receives six months of daylight, gradually heating up the planet to well over 100°C

claims.text: Earth's spin really is slowing: the length of the day has increased at an average rate of about 1.8 milliseconds per century (eclipse records, 720 BC to AD 2015).
claims.quote: the change in the length of the mean solar day (lod) increases at an average rate of +1.8 ms per century; has increased by an average of 1.8 milliseconds per century

claims.label: our sum, at today's average rate
claims.text: At that average rate, the day would take about 200 million years to get one hour longer.
claims.quote: the change in the length of the mean solar day (lod) increases at an average rate of +1.8 ms per century
claims.note: 3,600 s / 0.0018 s per century = 2,000,000 centuries = 200 million years. A linear extrapolation of today's average rate; the real rate fluctuates (the paper notes fluctuations about the trend). Labelled on the page.

claims.text: Earth will never actually stop rotating; its rate fluctuates but the trend is a very gradual slowdown.
claims.quote: even though fluctuations will continue, you can rest assured that Earth will never actually stop rotating

myths.myth: If Earth stopped, you'd be flung into space.
myths.truth: You'd keep moving sideways (east) at the ground's old speed, up to about 1,670 km/h at the equator; the danger is the sudden sideways motion, winds and water.

open_questions: The magnetic field claim (IFLScience: a non-rotating Earth has no field) is not used: not sourced to a geophysics paper.
IFLScience's '18.5 billion years for a day as long as a year' is not used: it does not follow from its own 1.7 ms/century figure (that gives about 1.9 trillion years).
